title: Mastery Challenge: World Geography
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of World Geography Levels 1–99 across the whole tree.
summary: Questions from across the tree: maps, coordinates, time and GPS, then people, cities, borders, languages, food, resources and migration. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The World Geography Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the whole tree, from reading a map to reading the planet's people. Level 1 started with a spinning globe; now see how much of it you can explain. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: World Geography: mastered
learned: Maps, coordinates, time zones and GPS
Land, oceans and how to read them
Where people live, and the cities, borders and languages they share
Food, resources, migration and a changing planet

questions.prompt: Africa is about 14 times bigger than Greenland, yet a classroom poster shows them as rivals. What kind of map is it probably?

options.label: An equal-area map
options.rationale: An equal-area map would show Africa far larger.

options.label: A topographic map
options.rationale: Contour maps show height, not world-scale sizes.

options.label: A globe
options.rationale: A globe keeps sizes true.

questions.explanation: Mercator's map inflates places far from the Equator, so Greenland balloons. An equal-area map would show Africa's true size.

questions.prompt: Two cities are 45° of longitude apart. In standard time, about how many hours apart are their clocks?

options.label: 1 hour
options.rationale: That would be 15° apart.

options.label: 6 hours
options.rationale: That would be 90° apart.

options.label: 45 hours
options.rationale: Each hour covers 15°, not 1°.

questions.explanation: Earth turns 15° of longitude every hour, so 45° apart is about 3 hours apart.

questions.prompt: Why does your phone need a fourth GPS satellite, not just three?

options.label: To correct its own less precise clock
To send its location back to space
options.rationale: Phones only listen; they never transmit to GPS satellites.

options.label: Because each satellite covers one quarter of Earth
options.rationale: Coverage is not the reason.

options.label: To find the date line
options.rationale: GPS gives latitude, longitude and altitude.

questions.explanation: The satellites' clocks are superb and the phone's isn't; the fourth satellite lets the phone correct its own clock.

questions.prompt: On a hiking map, the contour lines are packed tightly together. What should you expect there?

options.label: Flat, easy ground
options.rationale: That would be widely spaced lines.

options.label: A lake
options.rationale: Lines show elevation, not water.

options.label: A time zone border
options.rationale: Contours join points of equal elevation.

questions.explanation: Contour lines join points of equal elevation. Close together, they mean the ground rises fast: a steep slope.

questions.prompt: By the UN's count, when did the world population pass 8 billion?

options.rationale: Around then it was about 1 billion.
Far too early.
Too early.

questions.explanation: The UN marked 15 November 2022 as the day the world reached 8 billion people.

questions.prompt: A friend insists there are exactly 193 countries. What is the fairest reply?

options.label: That's the UN's member count; other lists add places like Kosovo or Taiwan
That's wrong: there are exactly 195
options.rationale: Even 195 is only one way of counting.

options.label: That was true before South Sudan joined in 2011
options.rationale: The count of 193 includes South Sudan.

options.label: Nobody has ever counted countries
options.rationale: The UN keeps an official member list.

questions.explanation: The UN has 193 members (195 with its observer states), and places like Kosovo and Taiwan are counted on some lists but not others.

questions.prompt: English three, German drei, Latin tres, Sanskrit trayas. What does this pattern show?

options.label: English borrowed the word from all of them
options.rationale: The words are inherited, not borrowed.

options.label: They are all spoken in the same country
options.rationale: They span Europe and South Asia.

options.label: Counting was invented in Germany
options.rationale: The shared root is far older.

questions.explanation: Words like these all come from one Proto-Indo-European root: evidence that the languages share one ancestor.

questions.prompt: Why does it matter so much that over 90% of rice is grown and eaten in Asia-Pacific?

options.label: Asia-Pacific has the fewest people
options.rationale: It has the most.

options.label: Rice cannot grow anywhere else
options.rationale: The point is who eats it.

options.label: The region holds about 60% of humanity
Rice is mostly fed to livestock
options.rationale: Rice feeds almost half of humanity directly.

questions.explanation: Rice feeds almost half of humanity because it grows right where about 60% of people live: the Asia-Pacific region.

questions.prompt: A poor country discovers huge oil reserves. What does the resource curse warn could happen?

options.label: It will certainly become rich
options.rationale: Resources do not guarantee wealth.

options.label: Its oil will run out within a year
options.rationale: The curse is about growth, not supply.

options.label: It must give the oil to its neighbors
options.rationale: Nothing like that is required.

options.label: It may grow more slowly, and the oil may spark conflict

questions.explanation: Countries rich in natural resources often grow more slowly, partly through conflict, unless they reinvest the money wisely, as Botswana did.

questions.prompt: War is a push factor. Where do most people pushed from home by conflict end up?

options.label: On another continent
options.rationale: Most stay much closer.

options.label: In the United States
options.rationale: It hosts the most migrants overall, but most displaced people never cross a border.

options.label: In megacities abroad
options.rationale: Most never leave their own countries.

questions.explanation: Of 123.2 million forcibly displaced people at the end of 2024, 83.4 million were displaced inside their own countries.
